rows.stem: The conversion of an alkyl halide into an alkene by alcoholic KOH is classified as
rows.solution:
The conversion is a DEHYDROHALOGENATION reaction.

Alcoholic potassium hydroxide supplies ALKOXIDE ions, which are strong BASES but bulky and rather poor nucleophiles. An alkoxide therefore attacks a \(\beta\) HYDROGEN rather than the carbon, and the halide leaves along with it — a hydrogen and a halogen are removed from ADJACENT carbons, which is exactly what dehydrohalogenation means:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{KOH(alc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

It is an ELIMINATION, so the substitution and addition options are both wrong in kind. And DEhydration is the loss of WATER, which would require a hydroxyl group in the substrate — there is none here.

AQUEOUS potassium hydroxide gives the substitution instead, producing an alcohol.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The oxidation state of Fe in \(\mathrm{[Fe(CO)_5]}\) is
rows.solution:
The oxidation state of iron is ZERO.

Carbon monoxide is a NEUTRAL ligand — it donates a lone pair from its carbon without carrying any charge — so five of them contribute nothing to the arithmetic. The complex itself is neutral, written with no charge outside the brackets:
\(x + 5(0) = 0\), giving \(x = 0\)

Metal carbonyls are the standard case of a metal in the zero oxidation state, and they are possible because carbon monoxide is both a good \(\sigma\) donor and a good \(\pi\) acceptor: it accepts back-donation from the metal's filled d orbitals, which relieves the electron density a zero-valent metal would otherwise carry.

\(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(CO)_6]}\) are the same case.

rows.stem: Among the following, which is the strongest base ?
rows.solution:
The strongest base is BENZYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2NH_2}\).

The decisive question is whether the nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised into the RING. In an ARYLamine it is — the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is spread over the ortho and para carbons and is less available to accept a proton. All three of the other options are arylamines.

Benzylamine is different: its nitrogen sits on a \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) group, ONE CARBON away from the ring, and that saturated carbon breaks the conjugation completely. The lone pair stays on the nitrogen, so benzylamine behaves like an ordinary aliphatic amine and is much the strongest base here.

Among the three arylamines the order still follows the substituent: p-toluidine's methyl group RELEASES density and makes it stronger than aniline, while p-nitroaniline's nitro group WITHDRAWS and makes it much the weakest.

rows.stem: The slope in the plot of \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) vs. time for a first order reaction is
rows.solution:
The slope is \(-k\).

For a first order reaction, integrating the rate law gives
\(\ln[\mathrm{R}] = \ln[\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)

Compare with \(y = c + mx\), taking \(y\) as \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) and \(x\) as \(t\): the intercept is \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]_0\) and the slope is \(-k\).

The slope is NEGATIVE because the reactant is being consumed, so the line falls; the rate constant is recovered as \(k = -\text{slope}\).

The factor of 2.303 in two of the options belongs to the version of the same equation written with COMMON logarithms, \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\), where the slope is \(-k/2{\cdot}303\). Here the plot uses the NATURAL logarithm, so no conversion factor appears.

rows.stem: An \(\alpha\)-helix is a structural feature of
rows.solution:
The \(\alpha\)-helix is a structural feature of POLYPEPTIDES.

It is one of the two SECONDARY structures a protein chain adopts, the other being the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet. The chain coils like a spring, and the coil is held by HYDROGEN BONDS between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of one peptide linkage and the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) of another further along the same chain.

The other three options are carbohydrates or nucleic acid units. Sucrose is a disaccharide and starch a polysaccharide, neither of which has peptide linkages to hydrogen bond between; nucleotides are the units of nucleic acids, whose own helix is a DOUBLE helix of two strands held by base pairing — a different structure with a different name.

rows.stem: Racemisation occurs in
rows.solution:
Racemisation occurs in the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction.

In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) the leaving group departs FIRST, giving a PLANAR carbocation. Being flat, that intermediate can be attacked by the nucleophile from EITHER FACE with equal ease, so the two enantiomers are formed in equal amounts and the product is optically inactive — a racemic mixture.

\(\mathrm{S_N}2\) gives the opposite result. There the nucleophile attacks from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group in a single step, with no intermediate at all, so the configuration is INVERTED and a single enantiomer results.

That difference in stereochemistry is one of the main pieces of evidence for the two mechanisms: observing racemisation identifies the unimolecular route as surely as observing inversion identifies the bimolecular one.

rows.stem: Value of Henry's constant \(\mathrm{K_H}\) :
rows.solution:
Henry's constant INCREASES WITH INCREASE IN TEMPERATURE.

Rearranging \(p = K_{\mathrm{H}}x\) gives \(x = p/K_{\mathrm{H}}\), so at a given pressure the amount dissolved is INVERSELY proportional to the constant: a larger \(K_{\mathrm{H}}\) means a LESS soluble gas.

Dissolving a gas is an EXOTHERMIC process, so by Le Chatelier's principle warming drives it backwards and the solubility FALLS. Less soluble means a larger constant, so \(K_{\mathrm{H}}\) rises with temperature.

The everyday consequence is that a warm fizzy drink goes flat faster than a cold one, and that warm river water holds less dissolved oxygen for fish.

rows.stem: Which of the following solutions of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) will have the highest value of molar conductivity ?
rows.solution:
The 0.01 M solution has the highest molar conductivity — the most DILUTE of the four.

Molar conductivity refers the conductance to one mole of electrolyte, however much solvent that mole is spread through:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}\)

On dilution the ions move further apart, so they drag on one another less and each moves more freely. The value therefore RISES as the concentration falls, climbing towards the limiting \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) at infinite dilution.

CONDUCTIVITY behaves the opposite way, falling on dilution because fewer ions occupy the fixed volume between the electrodes. The two quantities are easily confused, and this question is testing which one moves which way.

rows.stem: Which of the following reactions are feasible ?
rows.solution:
Only the FIRST reaction is feasible — bromoethane with sodium tert-butoxide.

Williamson's synthesis is an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, so the ALKYL HALIDE must be primary: the alkoxide has to reach the carbon from behind, and a crowded carbon blocks it.

In the first reaction the halide is bromoETHANE, a primary halide with an accessible carbon, so the bulky tert-butoxide can still attack it and the ether forms. The bulk of the ALKOXIDE does not matter nearly as much as the bulk of the halide.

In the second the roles are swapped: the halide is tert-butyl chloride, whose carbon is fully substituted and unreachable. The ethoxide, being a strong base as well as a nucleophile, removes a \(\beta\) hydrogen instead, and the product is 2-methylpropene — an alkene, not the ether.

The lesson is that an unsymmetrical ether must be built with the primary group as the HALIDE and the hindered group as the ALKOXIDE, never the other way round.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following is most reactive in nucleophilic addition reactions ?
rows.solution:
METHANAL, HCHO, is the most reactive.

Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition falls as the carbonyl carbon is made less positive and more crowded, and ALKYL GROUPS do both: each one RELEASES electron density inductively, reducing the positive charge, and each one physically blocks the nucleophile's approach.

Count the alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon. Methanal has NONE — only two hydrogens. Ethanal has one. Propanone has two, and butanone has two, one of which is larger.

So the order runs methanal, then the aldehyde, then the ketones, and methanal is the most reactive carbonyl compound there is — reactive enough that in water it exists largely as its hydrate.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following does not give aldol condensation reaction ?
rows.solution:
BENZALDEHYDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\), does not give the aldol condensation.

The aldol reaction begins with a base removing an \(\alpha\)-HYDROGEN — a hydrogen on the carbon NEXT TO the carbonyl — to give a carbanion, which then attacks another molecule's carbonyl.

Benzaldehyde has no such hydrogen. Its carbonyl carbon is attached directly to the benzene RING, and the ring carbons carry no hydrogen available in that position. With no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen there is no carbanion and no aldol.

The other three all have \(\alpha\)-hydrogens: ethanal on its methyl, cyclohexanecarbaldehyde on its ring carbon, and propanone on both methyls.

What benzaldehyde does instead with concentrated alkali is the CANNIZZARO reaction — the disproportionation open precisely to aldehydes lacking an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen.

rows.stem: For the reaction \(3\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}\), rate of reaction \(+\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is equal to
rows.solution:
For \(3\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{B}\),
\(+\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Build it from the stoichiometry. Each species is divided by its coefficient, reactants taking a minus sign because they are being consumed:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Multiplying through by 2 to isolate the term asked for:
\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

The physical content is that \(\mathrm{A}\) disappears FASTER than \(\mathrm{B}\) appears — three consumed for every two produced — so the fraction must be less than 1. The option with \(3/2\) has it inverted.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following characteristics of transition metals is associated with their catalytic activity ?
rows.solution:
Catalytic activity is associated with VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES.

A catalyst works by offering the reaction a lower-energy path, and a transition metal does that by moving between oxidation states: it accepts electrons from one reactant, passes them to another, and returns to its original state at the end. Iron in the Haber process and vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process both work this way.

The other three are genuine properties of transition metals, but none of them supplies a reaction path. Paramagnetism reflects unpaired electrons, colour reflects d-d transitions, and a high enthalpy of atomisation reflects strong metallic bonding — all consequences of the partly filled d subshell, none a mechanism for catalysis.

The one other real catalytic mechanism, ADSORPTION of reactants on the metal surface through vacant d orbitals, is not among the options.

rows.stem: The formula of the complex dichloridobis (ethane –1, 2-diamine) platinum (IV) nitrate is
rows.solution:
The formula is \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2](NO_3)_2}\).

Read the name from the inside out. The part BEFORE the metal names the ligands inside the coordination sphere: dichlorido gives two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), and bis(ethane-1,2-diamine) gives two neutral en. The part AFTER names what lies outside — nitrate.

Platinum is stated as \(+4\). Inside the sphere the two chlorido ligands give \(-2\), so the complex ION carries \(4 - 2 = +2\) and needs TWO nitrate ions outside to balance it.

The distractors move the nitrate inside the brackets, which the name forbids — anything inside would have been named before the metal. Only a counter ion is named at the end, after the metal's oxidation state.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Osmotic pressure is a colligative property.
Reason (R) : Osmotic pressure is proportional to the molality.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Osmotic pressure IS a colligative property: it depends on the NUMBER of solute particles and not on their nature.

But the Reason names the wrong concentration scale. Osmotic pressure is proportional to MOLARITY, not molality:
\(\Pi = CRT\)
where \(C\) is moles of solute per litre of SOLUTION.

That is in fact one of osmotic pressure's practical advantages — molarity is what a laboratory can prepare directly. The other colligative properties do use MOLALITY: \(\Delta T_f = K_f m\) and \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\), because those are measured over a range of temperature and molality does not change with it while molarity does.

So the Reason is not a slip of degree but a genuine mix-up between the two scales.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Conductivity decreases with decrease in concentration of electrolyte.
Reason (R) : Number of ions per unit volume that carry the current in a solution decreases on dilution.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

CONDUCTIVITY is the conductance of a FIXED VOLUME of solution — the amount held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. Diluting the solution puts fewer ions into that volume, so fewer charge carriers are available to carry the current between the electrodes, and the conductivity falls.

The Reason states exactly that mechanism, so it accounts for the Assertion completely.

MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY is the contrast, and it RISES on dilution — because it counts the ions from a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume, and dilution lets those ions move more freely. The two quantities move in opposite directions, and knowing which is being referred to a volume and which to an amount settles both.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Copper is a non-transition element.
Reason (R) : Copper has completely filled d-orbitals in its ground state.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Copper IS a transition element, so the Assertion fails on a point of definition.

The Reason is correct as a statement of fact: copper's ground state is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^1\), with a completely filled d subshell.

But that does not disqualify it, because the definition looks at the ION as well as the atom. A transition element is one with a partly filled d subshell in the neutral atom OR IN ONE OF ITS STABLE IONS — and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), copper's commonest ion, is \(3d^9\), which is partly filled. Copper accordingly shows all the characteristic behaviour: coloured compounds, variable oxidation state, catalytic activity.

ZINC is the element the Assertion would fit. It is \(3d^{10}4s^2\) as the atom and \(3d^{10}\) as the \(+2\) ion — full in BOTH — so zinc is genuinely not a transition element.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Nucleophilic substitution of iodoethane is easier than chloroethane.
Reason (R) : Bond enthalpy of C-I bond is less than that of C-Cl bond.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Iodoethane does undergo nucleophilic substitution more readily than chloroethane. With the same carbon skeleton in both, the only variable is the halogen.

The Reason gives the mechanism. In any nucleophilic substitution the carbon-halogen bond must BREAK, so the weaker that bond, the faster the reaction — and the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond enthalpy is about 238 kJ per mole against the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond's 339.

The bond weakens down the group because the halogen grows larger and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well. A second effect points the same way: the iodide ion, being the largest, spreads its charge best and is the more stable anion — the better leaving group in both senses.

So reactivity runs iodide, bromide, chloride, fluoride, and the fluoride is so unreactive it is hardly used for substitution at all.

rows.stem: The vapour pressure of pure liquid X and pure liquid Y at 25 °C are 120 mm Hg and 160 mm Hg respectively. If equal moles of X and Y are mixed to form an ideal solution, calculate the vapour pressure of the solution.
rows.solution:
An IDEAL solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole range of composition, so each component's partial pressure is its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction, and the total is their sum:
\(p_{\text{total}} = p_{\mathrm{X}}^{\,\circ}\,x_{\mathrm{X}} + p_{\mathrm{Y}}^{\,\circ}\,x_{\mathrm{Y}}\)

EQUAL MOLES of the two are mixed, so each mole fraction is \(0{\cdot}5\):
\(p_{\text{total}} = (120 \times 0{\cdot}5) + (160 \times 0{\cdot}5)\)
\(= 60 + 80\)

\(p_{\text{total}} = 140\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

With equal mole fractions the result is simply the ARITHMETIC MEAN of the two pure vapour pressures, which is a useful check: 140 lies exactly midway between 120 and 160.

Note also that the VAPOUR is richer in the more volatile component: \(y_{\mathrm{Y}} = 80/140 = 0{\cdot}57\) against \(x_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{\cdot}5\). That enrichment is the basis of fractional distillation.

rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(i) Mercury cell delivers a constant potential during its life time.
(ii) In the experimental determination of electrolytic conductance, Direct Current (DC) is not used.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the overall reaction of the mercury cell involves NO ION IN SOLUTION whose concentration can change.

The potential of any cell obeys the Nernst equation, and it drifts as the cell runs only when the reaction quotient shifts — that is, when something whose concentration appears in that quotient is consumed or produced.

The mercury cell's reaction is
\(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\)
and every species in it is a SOLID or a pure liquid, none of which enters the quotient at all. With nothing to shift, the potential holds at about \(1{\cdot}35\) V for the life of the cell — which is why it suits hearing aids and watches.

(ii) Because DIRECT CURRENT CHANGES THE COMPOSITION of the electrolytic solution.

A steady current in one direction ELECTROLYSES the solution: ions are discharged at the electrodes and products accumulate there. The concentration is then no longer what it was when the measurement began, and the electrodes become polarised by the layer of product on them — so the resistance being read is not the resistance of the solution that was put in.

Alternating current avoids both problems: the direction reverses hundreds of times a second, so whatever is deposited in one half cycle is taken back in the next and no net electrolysis occurs.

rows.stem: Define fuel cell with an example. What advantages do the fuel cells have over primary and secondary batteries ?
rows.solution:
A FUEL CELL is a galvanic cell in which the energy of COMBUSTION OF A FUEL is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy, the reactants being supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within the cell.

EXAMPLE: the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, used on the Apollo space flights. Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen reduced at the cathode, both on porous carbon electrodes containing a catalyst, with aqueous potassium hydroxide between them:
\(\mathrm{2H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

ADVANTAGES over primary and secondary batteries:

HIGH EFFICIENCY, around 70%, because the chemical energy goes straight to electricity instead of passing through heat, so the cell is not limited by the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine.

POLLUTION FREE — the only product is water, with no oxides of carbon, nitrogen or sulphur.

It does not RUN DOWN, since it is fed from outside and works as long as fuel is supplied — unlike a primary cell, which is discarded when exhausted, or a secondary one, which must be taken out of service to be recharged.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) The conversion of molecule A to B followed second order kinetics. If concentration of A increased to three times, how will it affect the rate of formation of B ?
(b) Define Pseudo first order reaction with an example.
rows.solution:
(a) The rate becomes NINE TIMES greater.

Second order kinetics in \(\mathrm{A}\) means
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2\)

Trebling the concentration multiplies the rate by \(3^2\):
\(\text{new rate} = k(3[\mathrm{A}])^2 = 9\,k[\mathrm{A}]^2\)

The square is what matters. A first order reaction would have trebled, and a zero order one would not have changed at all — so the factor the rate changes by identifies the order.

(b) A PSEUDO FIRST ORDER REACTION is one that appears from its stoichiometry to be of higher order but is found by measurement to follow FIRST ORDER kinetics.

It arises when ONE OF THE REACTANTS IS PRESENT IN LARGE EXCESS. Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds, so it may be treated as a constant and absorbed into the rate constant, leaving a dependence on one concentration alone.

EXAMPLE: the acid hydrolysis of an ester, where water is the solvent as well as a reactant:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{ester}][\mathrm{H_2O}] = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\)
The inversion of sucrose is another.

rows.stem:
Write the IUPAC names of the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{K_2[NiCl_4]}\)
rows.solution:
(i) The five ammine ligands are neutral and the nitrite gives \(-1\), so against an overall \(+2\) cobalt must be \(+3\). The nitrite is written \(-\mathrm{ONO}\), bound through OXYGEN, so it is named nitrito-O:
PENTAAMMINENITRITO-O-COBALT(III) ION

Its linkage isomer, bound through nitrogen, would be the nitro-N form — the two are different compounds with different colours.

(ii) The two potassium ions give \(+2\) and four chlorido ligands \(-4\), so nickel is \(+2\) and the complex is the ANION. An anionic complex takes the -ate ending on the metal:
POTASSIUM TETRACHLORIDONICKELATE(II)

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(i) What is a chelate complex ? Give one example.
(ii) What are heteroleptic complexes ? Give one example.
rows.solution:
(i) A CHELATE COMPLEX is one formed by a DIDENTATE or POLYDENTATE ligand — a ligand that binds the metal through two or more donor atoms at once, closing a RING that includes the metal atom.

EXAMPLE: \(\mathrm{[Co(ox)_3]^{3-}}\), in which three oxalate ions each bind through two of their oxygens, closing three five-membered rings. \(\mathrm{[Ni(en)_3]^{2+}}\) serves equally well.

Chelation confers extra stability, an effect large enough to have its own name — the chelate effect — and the more rings closed, the greater the stability.

(ii) HETEROLEPTIC COMPLEXES are those in which the metal is bound to MORE THAN ONE KIND of ligand.

EXAMPLE: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\), whose cobalt carries both ammine and chlorido ligands.

The contrast is a HOMOLEPTIC complex, bound to only one kind — \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) or \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\). Only a heteroleptic complex can show geometrical isomerism, since cis and trans need two kinds of ligand to distinguish.

rows.stem:
Write the chemical equation involved in the following reactions :
(a) Reimer-Tiemann reaction
(b) Acetylation of Salicylic acid
rows.solution:
(a) REIMER-TIEMANN REACTION. Chloroform with aqueous alkali generates DICHLOROCARBENE, which attacks the phenoxide ion at its ORTHO position; the intermediate is hydrolysed and acidification then frees the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)

The product is SALICYLALDEHYDE. The alkali is needed twice over — to make the carbene and to convert phenol into the more strongly activated phenoxide ion.

(b) ACETYLATION OF SALICYLIC ACID. Acetic anhydride acetylates the PHENOLIC hydroxyl, leaving the carboxyl group free:
\(\mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3COO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is ACETYLSALICYLIC ACID — aspirin. The point of masking the phenolic hydroxyl is medical: free salicylic acid irritates the stomach lining badly, and the ester is hydrolysed back in the body.

rows.stem:
Do the following conversions in not more than two steps :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3CN}\) to \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\) to \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\)
rows.solution:
(a) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbon of a NITRILE, giving an imine salt, and hydrolysis of that gives a KETONE:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{CH_3{-}C({=}NMgBr){-}CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}/\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_3}\)

Count the carbons: two in the nitrile plus one from the reagent gives three. Note that the intermediate is NOT hydrolysed to an amine — the magnesium salt of the imine breaks down at the carbon-nitrogen bond, releasing ammonia and leaving the carbonyl.

(b) DECARBOXYLATION removes the carboxyl group as carbonate, leaving a hydrocarbon with ONE CARBON FEWER. The acid is first converted to its sodium salt, which is then heated with soda lime — sodium hydroxide with calcium oxide:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH}\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

A hydrogen replaces the carboxyl group on the ring, so the seven-carbon acid gives six-carbon benzene.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(ii) Why ortho-nitrophenol is steam volatile while para-nitrophenol is not ?
rows.solution:
(i) MECHANISM OF ETHER FORMATION at 413 K, in three steps.

Step 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid, converting the poor leaving group \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into the good one \(-\mathrm{OH_2^+}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 2 — nucleophilic attack by a SECOND alcohol molecule. The oxygen of another ethanol attacks the carbon of the protonated alcohol, displacing water in a bimolecular step:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — deprotonation. The protonated ether sheds the extra proton, giving the ether and regenerating the acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_2CH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}O{-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The TEMPERATURE selects the product: at 443 K the protonated alcohol loses water to a carbocation instead, and the product is ethene.

(ii) Because o-nitrophenol has INTRAMOLECULAR hydrogen bonding while p-nitrophenol has INTERmolecular.

In the ORTHO isomer the nitro group and the hydroxyl group are close enough to bond to each OTHER within the SAME molecule — sometimes called chelation. That uses up the hydroxyl's bonding capacity, so the molecules do not associate with one another, and the compound is volatile enough to distil over with the steam.

In the PARA isomer the two groups are too far apart to reach each other, so the hydrogen bonding is between DIFFERENT molecules. They associate into larger aggregates, the compound is far less volatile, and it stays behind in the flask.

That difference in volatility is what steam distillation exploits to separate them.

rows.stem:
What happens when
(i) Anisole is treated with \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)/anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) ?
(ii) Phenol is oxidised with \(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7/H^+}\) ?
(iii) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\,C-OH}\) is heated with Cu/573 K ?
Write chemical equation in support of your answer.
rows.solution:
(i) Anisole with methyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride is a Friedel-Crafts ALKYLATION. The methoxy group is ACTIVATING and ORTHO, PARA directing, so a mixture of the two isomers results:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3O{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{p\text{-}CH_3O{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3}\)
The products are 2-methylanisole and 4-methylanisole, the para predominating because the ortho position is crowded by the methoxy group already there.

(ii) Phenol with acidified sodium dichromate is OXIDISED to a QUINONE — a conjugated diketone in which the ring loses its aromatic character:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7}} \mathrm{C_6H_4O_2}\)
The product is BENZOQUINONE, a ring carrying two \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) groups at opposite corners with two double bonds between them.

(iii) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol over copper at 573 K is DEHYDRATED, not dehydrogenated:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{Cu}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is 2-METHYLPROPENE.

The reason is that a TERTIARY alcohol has no hydrogen on its carbinol carbon, so the dehydrogenation route open to primary and secondary alcohols — which would give an aldehyde or ketone — is closed to it. The same catalyst at the same temperature therefore gives three different products from the three classes.

rows.stem:
Answer any 3 of the following :
(a) Which isomer of \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) gives a single monochloro compound \(\mathrm{C_5H_9Cl}\) in bright sunlight ?
(b) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction :
2-Bromopentane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane
(c) Why p-dichlorobenzene has higher melting point than those of ortho- and meta-isomers ?
(d) Identify A and B in the following :
\(\text{bromocyclobutane} \xrightarrow[\text{Dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{B}\)
rows.solution:
(a) CYCLOPENTANE.

A single monochloro product requires ALL the hydrogens in the molecule to be EQUIVALENT, so that whichever one is replaced gives the same compound. Cyclopentane is a ring of five \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups — all ten hydrogens sit in identical environments, and replacing any of them gives chlorocyclopentane.

Any open-chain isomer of \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) is an alkene, and would ADD chlorine rather than substitute; a methylcyclobutane or dimethylcyclopropane would have several different kinds of hydrogen and give a mixture.

(b) Increasing reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N}2\):
2-BROMO-2-METHYLBUTANE < 2-BROMOPENTANE < 1-BROMOPENTANE

The bimolecular route requires the nucleophile to reach the carbon from the side OPPOSITE the leaving group, so the rate is governed by ACCESSIBILITY. 1-Bromopentane is PRIMARY and nearly unobstructed; 2-bromopentane is SECONDARY, with two alkyl groups in the way; 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is TERTIARY, with three, and is essentially unreactive by this route.

Steric hindrance, not electronics, decides — and the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) order runs exactly the opposite way.

(c) Because the PARA isomer is the most SYMMETRICAL of the three, so its molecules pack into the crystal lattice more closely and more regularly.

A better packed lattice takes more energy to break down, so p-dichlorobenzene melts highest.

Note that the argument concerns the SOLID state only. BOILING points follow dipole moment instead, and there the para isomer — being symmetrical and therefore non-polar — comes out LOWEST. The same symmetry raises one and lowers the other.

(d) Magnesium in dry ether converts the halide into a GRIGNARD REAGENT:
\(\mathrm{A} = \) cyclobutylmagnesium bromide, \(\mathrm{C_4H_7{-}MgBr}\)

Water then destroys it. The carbon bonded to magnesium carries a large partial NEGATIVE charge and behaves as a carbanion, so it seizes a proton from the water:
\(\mathrm{B} = \) cyclobutane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\)

This is why a Grignard reagent must be prepared under anhydrous conditions — the reaction that makes \(\mathrm{B}\) here is exactly the one that would destroy the reagent before it could be used.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
A first order reaction is 50% complete in 30 minutes at 300 K and in 10 minutes at 320 K. Calculate activation energy \((\mathrm{E_a})\) for the reaction.
\([\mathrm{R} = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}]\)
[Given : log 2 = 0.3010, log 3 = 0.4771, log 4 = 0.6021]
rows.solution:
"50% complete" is the HALF-LIFE, so each rate constant follows directly.

Step 1 — the two rate constants:
\(k_1 = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{30}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\) at 300 K, and \(k_2 = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{10}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\) at 320 K

Their RATIO is all that enters, and the 0.693 cancels:
\(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3\)

Step 2 — the Arrhenius equation in its two-point form:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]\)
\(\log 3 = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303 \times 8{\cdot}314}\left[\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{320}\right]\)

The bracket is \(\dfrac{320 - 300}{300 \times 320} = \dfrac{20}{96000}\), so
\(E_a = \dfrac{0{\cdot}4771 \times 19{\cdot}147 \times 300 \times 320}{20}\)

\(E_a = 43848\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is about \(43{\cdot}85\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that the half-lives never had to be turned into rate constants at all — only their ratio was needed, and that is the inverse ratio of the half-lives. The temperatures, by contrast, must be in kelvin, since their product appears in the bracket.

rows.stem:
When 19.5 g of \(\mathrm{F-CH_2-COOH}\) (Molar mass = 78 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)), is dissolved in 500 g of water, the depression in freezing point is observed to be 1°C. Calculate the degree of dissociation of \(\mathrm{F-CH_2-COOH}\).
[Given : \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = 1.86 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
The acid DISSOCIATES, so the observed depression is larger than the formula predicts and the van't Hoff factor exceeds 1.

Step 1 — the van't Hoff factor, from the measured depression:
\(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,\dfrac{w_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{w_A}\)
\(1 = i \times 1{\cdot}86 \times \dfrac{19{\cdot}5}{78} \times \dfrac{1000}{500}\)
\(1 = i \times 1{\cdot}86 \times 0{\cdot}25 \times 2 = i \times 0{\cdot}93\)

\(i = 1{\cdot}075\)

Step 2 — degree of dissociation. Fluoroethanoic acid ionises into TWO particles, \(\mathrm{FCH_2COO^-}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\), so \(n = 2\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}075 - 1}{2 - 1}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}075\), that is 7.5%

The smallness of the figure is the point: fluoroethanoic acid is a WEAK acid, and even with fluorine's strong electron withdrawal only about one molecule in thirteen is ionised at this concentration. Note also that \(i\) exceeding 1 is what identifies dissociation — association would have put it BELOW 1.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the geometrical isomers of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\). Which geometrical isomer of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\) is not optically active and why ?
(b) Write the hybridisation and magnetic behaviour of \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\).
[Given : Atomic number of Co = 27]
rows.solution:
(a) The complex is octahedral with two chlorido ligands and two bidentate diamines, so the two chlorides may sit adjacent or opposite.

CIS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands on ADJACENT positions, with the two diamine ligands spanning the remaining four.
TRANS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands directly OPPOSITE each other along one axis, with the two chelate rings lying in the plane between them.

The TRANS isomer is NOT optically active, because it has a PLANE OF SYMMETRY — its mirror image is superimposable on itself, so it cannot rotate plane polarised light. The cis isomer has no such plane and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

A note on the charge as printed. Two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) and the diamines are neutral, so a \(+2\) ion would put cobalt at \(+4\); the familiar ion is \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\), with cobalt(III). The marking scheme accepts either charge written over the isomers, so nothing in the answer turns on it.

(b) Cobalt is atomic number 27, so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\) — six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\).

FLUORIDE is a WEAK FIELD ligand: the splitting it produces is smaller than the pairing energy, so it cannot force the electrons to pair. No inner \(3d\) orbital is left vacant, and bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set.

HYBRIDISATION: \(sp^3d^2\) — an outer orbital, high spin complex.
MAGNETIC BEHAVIOUR: PARAMAGNETIC, with FOUR unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is the contrast — the same \(3d^6\) ion, but with a strong field ligand it is \(d^2sp^3\) and diamagnetic.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Write the name of the product when an aldehyde reacts with excess alcohol in presence of dry HCl.
rows.context: The carbon – oxygen double bond is polarised in aldehydes and ketones due to higher electronegativity of oxygen relative to carbon. Therefore they undergo nucleophilic addition reactions with a number of nucleophiles such as HCN, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\), alcohols, ammonia derivatives and Grignard reagents. Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents as compared to ketones. The carbonyl group of carboxylic acid does not give reactions of aldehydes and ketones. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
The product is an ACETAL.

An alcohol adds ONCE to an aldehyde to give a HEMIACETAL, a carbon bearing both an \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and an \(-\mathrm{OR}\). With EXCESS alcohol and dry hydrogen chloride the reaction goes a step further: the hemiacetal's hydroxyl is replaced by a second alkoxy group, and water is lost.
\(\mathrm{RCHO} + 2\mathrm{R'OH} \xrightarrow{\text{dry }\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{RCH(OR')_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The acetal carbon therefore carries TWO alkoxy groups. Acetals are stable to alkali but hydrolysed back by aqueous acid, which is why they are used as PROTECTING GROUPS for a carbonyl while some other part of a molecule is worked on.

rows.stem: Why carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than phenol ?
rows.context: The carbon – oxygen double bond is polarised in aldehydes and ketones due to higher electronegativity of oxygen relative to carbon. Therefore they undergo nucleophilic addition reactions with a number of nucleophiles such as HCN, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\), alcohols, ammonia derivatives and Grignard reagents. Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents as compared to ketones. The carbonyl group of carboxylic acid does not give reactions of aldehydes and ketones. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
Because the CARBOXYLATE ion is more resonance stabilised than the PHENOXIDE ion.

When a carboxylic acid loses its proton, the negative charge is delocalised over TWO EQUIVALENT OXYGEN ATOMS. The two resonance structures are identical, and the charge is shared equally between two electronegative atoms — which carry it comfortably.

When phenol loses its proton, the charge is delocalised into the benzene RING, onto CARBON atoms, which are far less electronegative and hold it much less comfortably. The resonance structures involved are also not equivalent to one another, and they disturb the ring's aromatic stability.

The more stable the anion, the more readily the parent gives up its proton — so the carboxylic acid is the stronger acid, \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 4.76 against phenol's 10.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their reactivity towards \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\) :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CO-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)
(ii) Write a chemical test to distinguish between propanal and propanone.
rows.context: The carbon – oxygen double bond is polarised in aldehydes and ketones due to higher electronegativity of oxygen relative to carbon. Therefore they undergo nucleophilic addition reactions with a number of nucleophiles such as HCN, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\), alcohols, ammonia derivatives and Grignard reagents. Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents as compared to ketones. The carbonyl group of carboxylic acid does not give reactions of aldehydes and ketones. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing reactivity towards \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\):
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CO{-}CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

A Grignard reagent attacks the carbonyl carbon as a nucleophile, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and alkyl groups do both, releasing electron density inductively and blocking the approach.

Ethanal has ONE alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon and a hydrogen; propanone has TWO methyls; and the tert-butyl ketone has a methyl and a bulky tert-butyl group, which is both the most electron-releasing and much the most obstructive.

(ii) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warm each with iodine and sodium hydroxide.

PROPANONE, \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}\) — a methyl KETONE — gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform, \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\). PROPANAL has no methyl group attached to its carbonyl carbon and gives none.

Tollens' reagent serves equally well the other way round: propanal, being an aldehyde, deposits a silver mirror while propanone does not react.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the main product in the following :
(i) 3-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2NCONHNH_2}}\)
rows.context: The carbon – oxygen double bond is polarised in aldehydes and ketones due to higher electronegativity of oxygen relative to carbon. Therefore they undergo nucleophilic addition reactions with a number of nucleophiles such as HCN, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\), alcohols, ammonia derivatives and Grignard reagents. Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents as compared to ketones. The carbonyl group of carboxylic acid does not give reactions of aldehydes and ketones. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (i)'s substrate is printed ONLY as a drawing on idx 18 — a cyclohexane ring with a doubly-bonded O at the top vertex and \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) on the vertex two bonds clockwise from it (the 3-position). Sub-part (ii)'s substrate is a drawn benzene ring bearing \(-\mathrm{CHO}\). The naming above is a reading of the drawing, and the ring POSITION is what it turns on, so the real crop should be attached. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) Tollens' reagent is a MILD oxidising agent, and it is SELECTIVE: it oxidises an ALDEHYDE and leaves a KETONE alone.

The substrate carries both — an aldehyde on one ring carbon and a ketone on another — so only the aldehyde is attacked. The reagent is alkaline, so the product is the CARBOXYLATE ion rather than the free acid.

Product: the cyclohexanone ring still carrying its \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\), with the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) now a \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\).

A ketone has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon to be removed, which is why it survives — and that selectivity is what makes Tollens' a test for aldehydes.

(ii) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water, to give the SEMICARBAZONE:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}CO{-}NH{-}NH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5CH{=}N{-}NH{-}CONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Note which nitrogen attacks. Semicarbazide has TWO \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups, but the one attached directly to the carbonyl has its lone pair delocalised onto that carbonyl's oxygen and is a poor nucleophile. Only the TERMINAL one, separated from the carbonyl by an intervening nitrogen, is free to react.

rows.stem: The penta-acetate of glucose does not react with Hydroxylamine. What does it indicate ?
rows.context: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones. They are also called saccharides. All those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollen's reagent are referred to as reducing sugars. Glucose, the most important source of energy for mammals, is obtained by the hydrolysis of starch. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. Proteins are the polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids and perform various structural and dynamic functions in the organisms. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases.
rows.solution:
It indicates the ABSENCE OF A FREE ALDEHYDE GROUP in glucose pentaacetate.

Hydroxylamine condenses with a carbonyl group to give an oxime, and glucose ITSELF gives that reaction readily — which is one of the proofs that glucose contains a carbonyl group.

Acetylating all five hydroxyls, however, locks the molecule in its CYCLIC form: the hydroxyl at the anomeric carbon is now an acetate and can no longer leave, so the ring cannot open to the straight-chain form and no aldehyde is ever exposed.

The observation is one of the pieces of evidence that glucose exists predominantly as a CYCLIC HEMIACETAL rather than as the open-chain aldehyde — the open chain must be reachable for the aldehyde reactions to occur at all.

rows.stem: Why cannot vitamin C be stored in our body ?
rows.context: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones. They are also called saccharides. All those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollen's reagent are referred to as reducing sugars. Glucose, the most important source of energy for mammals, is obtained by the hydrolysis of starch. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. Proteins are the polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids and perform various structural and dynamic functions in the organisms. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases.
rows.solution:
Because vitamin C is WATER SOLUBLE, so any excess is EXCRETED THROUGH THE URINE rather than being laid down anywhere.

The body has no fatty tissue in which to hold a water-soluble compound, so no reserve accumulates and a regular dietary supply is required.

The FAT-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — are the contrast: they are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue and need not be supplied daily. The practical consequence for vitamin C is historical: scurvy appeared on long sea voyages after only a few weeks without fresh food.

rows.stem:
Define the following as related to proteins :
(i) Peptide linkage
(ii) Denaturation
rows.context: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones. They are also called saccharides. All those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollen's reagent are referred to as reducing sugars. Glucose, the most important source of energy for mammals, is obtained by the hydrolysis of starch. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. Proteins are the polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids and perform various structural and dynamic functions in the organisms. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases.
rows.solution:
(i) A PEPTIDE LINKAGE is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) that joins two amino acids. The carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond formed between that carbon and that nitrogen is the peptide linkage.

It is what builds a protein from its residues, and the sequence those bonds fix is the protein's primary structure.

(ii) DENATURATION is the LOSS OF A PROTEIN'S BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY when its native structure is destroyed by a change in temperature, pH or some other physical or chemical condition.

The weak forces holding the chain in shape are disrupted, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds: the SECONDARY and TERTIARY structures are destroyed while the PRIMARY structure survives intact, since no peptide bond is broken. Coagulation of egg white on boiling is the everyday instance, and it is irreversible.

rows.stem:
Define the following as related to carbohydrates :
(i) Anomers
(ii) Glycosidic linkage
rows.context: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones. They are also called saccharides. All those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollen's reagent are referred to as reducing sugars. Glucose, the most important source of energy for mammals, is obtained by the hydrolysis of starch. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. Proteins are the polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids and perform various structural and dynamic functions in the organisms. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases.
rows.solution:
(i) ANOMERS are a pair of cyclic sugars that differ ONLY in the configuration at the ANOMERIC CARBON — \(\mathrm{C_1}\) in an ALDOSE such as glucose, \(\mathrm{C_2}\) in a KETOSE such as fructose.

That carbon becomes a new stereocentre when the ring closes, and its hydroxyl can end up on either side: BELOW the plane in the \(\alpha\) form, ABOVE it in the \(\beta\) form. Everything else about the two molecules is identical.

In solution the two interconvert through the open-chain form, which is what MUTAROTATION is — the slow drift of the observed rotation towards an equilibrium value.

(ii) A GLYCOSIDIC LINKAGE is the linkage joining two monosaccharides THROUGH AN OXYGEN ATOM, formed by the loss of a molecule of water between them.

It runs from the anomeric carbon of one sugar to a carbon of the next — \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_4}\) in maltose. It is what builds disaccharides and polysaccharides, and whether the disaccharide is REDUCING depends on whether the linkage leaves an anomeric carbon free.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(I) Account for the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{E^o}\) value for \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\) couple is much more positive than that for \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\).
(ii) \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is colourless whereas \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is coloured in an aqueous solution.
(iii) Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
(II) Write the chemical equations for the preparation of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) from \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).
rows.solution:
(I)(i) Because reducing each ion produces a different degree of stability.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is \(3d^4\), and gaining one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is the exactly HALF-FILLED \(3d^5\) — an arrangement of considerable extra stability. Manganese(III) therefore takes an electron very readily, which is what a large POSITIVE potential means.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\), and in an octahedral aqueous environment that is the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Chromium(III) is already settled and has little inclination to be reduced further, so its potential is small and negative.

The result is that manganese(III) is a powerful oxidising agent while chromium(II) is a powerful reducing agent.

(ii) Because \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) has NO UNPAIRED ELECTRON in its d orbitals while \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) has one.

Colour in these ions comes from a d-d TRANSITION: an electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set of split d orbitals to the upper. That requires an electron to move and a vacancy to receive it.

Scandium(III) is \(3d^0\) — empty, with no electron to promote — so it is colourless. Titanium(III) is \(3d^1\), and that single electron can make the jump, so its aqueous solution is violet.

(iii) Because the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals of the actinoids lie at COMPARABLE ENERGIES.

Electrons from all three sets are therefore available for bonding, and there is no strong threshold at which the supply stops — uranium runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\), and neptunium and plutonium reach \(+7\).

The lanthanoids are the contrast: there the \(4f\) orbitals are buried well below the valence level and take no part, so nearly all lanthanoids are restricted to \(+3\).

(II) PREPARATION OF POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE FROM PYROLUSITE, in two stages.

Stage 1 — fusion. Manganese dioxide is fused with potassium hydroxide in the presence of air or another oxidising agent, and manganese is raised from \(+4\) to \(+6\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The dark green manganate is formed.

Stage 2 — disproportionation in acid, in which manganese goes both up to \(+7\) and down to \(+4\):
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Industrially the second stage is done by ELECTROLYTIC oxidation of the manganate instead, which converts all of it rather than only two-thirds.

rows.stem:
(I) Account for the following :
(i) Transition metals form alloys.
(ii) \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) is a strong oxidising agent.
(II) Write one similarity and one difference between chemistry of Lanthanoids and Actinoids.
(III) Complete the following ionic equation :
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(I)(i) Because transition metals have NEARLY THE SAME ATOMIC SIZE.

An alloy forms when atoms of one metal replace atoms of another in its crystal lattice, and that substitution works smoothly only if the two kinds of atom are of comparable size — a much larger or smaller atom distorts the lattice and will not be accommodated.

Across a transition series the radii change very little, because each added electron enters an inner \((n-1)d\) orbital and shields the added nuclear charge fairly well. Neighbouring transition metals are therefore near-interchangeable in a lattice.

(ii) Because \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) reverts to the COMMON \(+3\) OXIDATION STATE.

Nearly all lanthanoids are stable at \(+3\), and cerium(IV) reaches that state by GAINING one electron — which is what being an oxidising agent means. The driving force is simply that \(+3\) is where the series prefers to sit.

Cerium(IV) is accordingly used in volumetric analysis, and it is one of the few lanthanoids with a stable state other than \(+3\).

(II) SIMILARITY: both lanthanoids and actinoids show a CONTRACTION in atomic and ionic radii across their series, and both are stable in the \(+3\) oxidation state.

DIFFERENCE: lanthanoids are mainly NON-RADIOACTIVE — promethium is the exception — whereas ALL actinoids are radioactive. Another difference: actinoids show a much wider range of oxidation states, because their \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lie close in energy.

(III) In alkali the dichromate ion is converted to the CHROMATE ion, and the orange colour turns yellow:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Check the balance: chromium 2 both sides; oxygen \(7 + 2 = 9\) on the left against \(8 + 1 = 9\); hydrogen 2 both sides; charge \(-2 - 2 = -4\) on the left against \(2 \times (-2) = -4\).

This is a pH-controlled EQUILIBRIUM, not a redox change — chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout — and acid reverses it.

rows.stem:
(I) Give reasons :
(i) Aniline on nitration gives good amount of m-nitroaniline, though \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is o/p directing in electrophilic substitution reactions.
(ii) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\,NH}\) is more basic than \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) in an aqueous solution.
(iii) Ammonolysis of alkyl halides is not a good method to prepare pure primary amines.
(II) Write the reaction involved in the following :
(i) Carbyl amine test
(ii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
rows.solution:
(I)(i) Because the nitrating mixture is strongly ACIDIC, and it PROTONATES the amino group.

Aniline's \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is indeed ortho, para directing — but in the presence of sulphuric acid a large part of the aniline is converted to the ANILINIUM ion, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3}\).

That positively charged group is strongly DEACTIVATING and META directing, so whatever nitration it undergoes goes meta. The product is therefore a mixture, with a substantial amount — about half — of m-nitroaniline alongside the ortho and para isomers.

The way round it is to PROTECT the amino group by acetylation first: the amide is far less basic, is not protonated, and nitrates cleanly at the para position.

(ii) Because of a COMBINATION of the INDUCTIVE effect and the SOLVATION effect, which pull in opposite directions.

Methyl groups RELEASE electron density onto the nitrogen, making its lone pair more available — and on that count alone the tertiary amine should be the strongest base.

But the CATION formed on protonation must also be stabilised by HYDROGEN BONDING to the surrounding water, and that needs hydrogens on the nitrogen. Trimethylamine's cation has only ONE, and its three methyl groups crowd the water away besides; dimethylamine's has TWO.

The secondary amine is the compromise that wins, and in aqueous solution the observed order for methylamines is secondary, then primary, then tertiary. In the GAS PHASE, with no solvent, only the inductive effect operates and the tertiary amine is strongest.

(iii) Because ammonolysis gives a MIXTURE OF AMINES that is difficult to separate.

Ammonia attacks the alkyl halide to give a primary amine, but that amine is itself a BETTER nucleophile than ammonia, so it attacks more halide to give the secondary amine, then the tertiary, and finally the quaternary ammonium salt.

A large excess of ammonia makes the primary amine PREDOMINATE, by probability rather than by chemistry, but all four products are still present and their boiling points are close.

GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS avoids the problem entirely, giving a pure primary amine — though only an aliphatic one.

(II)(i) CARBYLAMINE TEST. A primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic alkali gives an isocyanide, detected by its exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R{-}NC} + 3\mathrm{NaCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
It works only for PRIMARY amines, because forming the isocyanide needs BOTH nitrogen hydrogens.

(II)(ii) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, made acidic by the two flanking carbonyls; the anion then displaces halide from the alkyl halide; and hydrolysis frees the amine. It fails for aromatic amines, because an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution.

rows.stem:
(I) Write the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCN}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O/H^+}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{C}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe/HCl}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[273\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{C}\)
(II) Why aniline does not undergo Friedal-Crafts reaction ?
(III) Arrange the following in increasing order of their boiling point :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\)
rows.solution:
(I)(i) Copper(I) cyanide replaces the diazonium group by cyanide — the Sandmeyer reaction:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CN}\), benzonitrile

Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile goes all the way to the carboxylic acid:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), benzoic acid

Heating an acid with ammonia gives the ammonium salt and then, on further heating, the AMIDE:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide

(I)(ii) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid at 273 K diazotises it, and the salt SURVIVES at that temperature because the ring delocalises the positive charge:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

Ethanol reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by hydrogen and being itself oxidised to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_6}\), benzene

(II) Because ANILINE FORMS A SALT with the Lewis acid anhydrous aluminium chloride.

The nitrogen's lone pair is exactly what a Lewis acid seeks, so the catalyst bonds to it and is tied up — unavailable to generate the electrophile. Worse, the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE charge, which makes it strongly deactivating and meta directing rather than the powerful activator it was.

(III) Increasing boiling point:
\((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} < \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)

Boiling point here tracks INTERMOLECULAR HYDROGEN BONDING. Triethylamine has NO hydrogen on its nitrogen at all, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to one another and are held only by weak dipole-dipole forces — despite being much the heaviest of the three. Ethylamine has TWO such hydrogens. And ethanol's hydrogen sits on OXYGEN, which is more electronegative than nitrogen and makes the strongest bonds of all.

rows.stem:
(a) Conductivity of \(2 \times 10^{-3}\) M methanoic acid is \(8 \times 10^{-5}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation if \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm{o}}\) for methanoic acid is 404 S \(\mathrm{cm^2 mol^{-1}}\).
(b) Calculate the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{G}^{\circ}\) and log \(\mathrm{K_c}\) for the given reaction at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Ni_{(s)}} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+_{(aq)}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ni^{2+}_{(aq)}} + 2\mathrm{Ag_{(s)}}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} = -0.25\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ag^+/Ag}} = +0.80\) V
\(1\mathrm{F} = 96500\) C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
(a) MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY. Refer the conductivity to one mole of electrolyte, so the concentration divides out:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 40\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION. The ratio of the measured value to the limiting one, which is what the electrolyte would show if fully dissociated:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{40}{404}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}099\), about 9.9%

The smallness of the figure is the point: methanoic acid is a WEAK electrolyte, and at this concentration only about one molecule in ten is ionised at any moment. For a STRONG electrolyte the ratio would be close to 1, which is why this method of finding \(\alpha\) applies to weak electrolytes alone.

(b) Silver has the more positive potential, so it is the cathode and nickel the anode:
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}80 - (-0{\cdot}25) = 1{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{V}\)

Nickel goes from 0 to \(+2\), so TWO electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\).

FREE ENERGY CHANGE:
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -2 \times 96500 \times 1{\cdot}05\)
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -202650\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(-202{\cdot}65\) kJ \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)

EQUILIBRIUM CONSTANT:
\(\log K_c = \dfrac{n\,E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}}{0{\cdot}059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}05}{0{\cdot}059}\)
\(\log K_c = 35{\cdot}6\)

The signs are the check: a positive cell potential must give a negative free energy change and a very large equilibrium constant, and \(K_c \approx 10^{35{\cdot}6}\) means the reaction goes essentially to completion.
